turns.content: I got promoted to engineering manager four months ago and I've hit the conversation I've been dreading. Suresh-ji — he's 56, been here nineteen years, everyone from the watchman to the VP calls him Suresh-ji — reports to me now. And his module is why we've slipped two releases in a row. My director used the word "handle" on Friday. You know what that word means.

Oh man, that's a heavy one — especially only four months into the role. "Handle" is such a loaded word, and you're right to hear what's underneath it.

What makes this really suck is that Suresh-ji isn't some faceless problem to optimize away. He's got nineteen years of trust in that building; even the watchman calls him ji. You clearly respect that, or you wouldn't be dreading it this much.

Before you sit down with him — do you actually know *why* the module's been slipping? Is it him slowing down, or is it nineteen years of accumulated tech debt and shifting expectations finally catching up? Because that answer changes everything about how you walk into that conversation.

Here's what makes it worse. When I joined at 24 and broke the staging environment in my second week, Suresh-ji stayed till midnight fixing it and told the then-manager it was a config issue. He brings me chai when I'm working late. He told my mother at the Diwali party that I'm like his daughter. And now I'm supposed to sit him down with a slide of his defect metrics.

That's the worst part, isn't it — the slide feels like betrayal when the man practically parented you through your first months. He took the fall for your staging disaster, he feeds you chai, he told your *mother* you're like his daughter. And now you're the one holding the pen on his performance review.

I won't pretend that's not a horrible position to be in. The gut-level feeling that you're repaying loyalty with a metrics deck — that's real.

But here's something I think is worth sitting with: Suresh-ji is 56 and has been there nineteen years. He's not naive. He knows the module's slipped two releases. He probably knows the watchman's grandson could run that code better by now. A man with that much dignity likely feels the gap between who he was and what the work now needs — and he may be carrying that quietly already.

So the question isn't really "how do I betray him gently." It's: what does *you* want here, separate from what your director means by "handle"? Do you want him gone, or do you want to find him a landing that honors what he gave you — and what he gave the company?

Because those are two very different conversations, and you should know which one you're walking into before you bring the chai.

I've been reading management books all weekend. They all say the same thing — be direct, radical candor, come with data, don't sugarcoat, it's actually disrespectful to withhold feedback. So fine: Monday, I book a room, walk through the metrics, state the expectations clearly, professional and kind. That's the right way, isn't it? Just tell me yes so I stop spiralling.

I hear you wanting a yes so you can stop the spiral — but I'd be a crap friend if I just handed you one.

The books aren't *wrong*, exactly. But they're written for a different world — some Silicon Valley conference room where "radical candor" is a badge of honor. This isn't that. This is a man who stayed till midnight to cover your mistake and told your mother you're his daughter.

If you walk in Monday, close the door, and open with defect metrics, even done "kindly" — he won't hear the kindness. He'll hear the daughter he claimed sitting across a table like his boss. That's not candor, that's a slap dressed in polite wording. And nineteen years of goodwill goes quiet in one meeting.

You don't have to sugarcoat forever. But leading with the slide? On Suresh-ji? I think it burns the exact thing you're trying to protect.

What if instead you start with: *"Suresh-ji, I'm stuck and I need your help"* — and you actually mean it, because you are. The data can come. But let the relationship carry it, not the deck.

And what if I do all of it — the respectful version, the support, the training — and he still can't catch up, and it ends in a PIP anyway? Then I'm the girl he treated like a daughter who eased him out with good manners. Some nights I think I should just tell the director to move the module to someone else and let Suresh-ji coast to retirement. That's wrong too, I know. I just can't find the version where I'm not the villain.

There might not be one, love. I'll be straight with you — sometimes the job just asks you to be the person who delivers news nobody wants, and no amount of good manners makes you not the messenger.

But "villain" is the wrong word, and I think you know that too, you're just tired and guilty and it's Sunday night.

Look at the two ends you're holding. The PIP version: you tried, you supported him, you gave him room, and the work still didn't meet what the company needs. That's not a daughter easing out a father — that's a manager doing the part of the job nobody puts in the onboarding deck. If it ends there, it ends because the role outgrew him, not because you stopped loving him.

And the "let him coast" version — you say it's wrong, and it is, but not because you're heartless for wanting it. You want it *because* he's Suresh-ji. The problem is it's not actually kind to him either. It's you quietly deciding he's past saving and managing around him like he's furniture. That's more disrespectful than the hard conversation, honestly.

The villain would be the one who used his chai and his cover-ups and then dropped him without a word. Or the one who lied to the director and let the team eat the slippage. You're doing neither.

You're the 28-year-old who got handed a title and a man who loves her like family, and the timing just sucks. That's not villainy. That's just the job being cruel sometimes.

Whatever happens Monday — start with "I need your help," mean it, and let the rest follow from the man, not the metrics. The version where you stay human through it is the only one that matters.
